5) Evidence: we provide exportable CSVs, Grafana snapshots, and a short attestation document.

Hi Ben,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Before we proceed to procurement I need to confirm a few privacy/data-use items so I can clear this with our legal and InfoSec teams. Please see the list below — short answers are fine but we may ask for contract language after that.

1) Training opt-out (no-train): can you commit that Orbital Health customer content will not be used to improve or retrain Redwood models unless we explicitly opt in? If yes, is that a contractual commitment or a technical setting (or both)?

2) Prompt/response ownership: we need language that clarifies Orbital retains ownership of prompts and the model outputs generated from our data — are there any usage rights Redwood requires for model improvement or benchmarking?

3) Subprocessors: please provide your current list of subprocessors (or a link) and your process for notifying us of additions. Any subprocessor that will see customer content must be declared.

4) Cross-border transfers and legal basis: our data residency requirement is US-only for PHI-adjacent workloads. If Redwood routes any requests outside the US, we need to understand safeguards (SCCs, Data Privacy Framework, or hosting options).

5) Evidence: SOC 2 report excerpt (non-redacted) and a point of contact for security questionnaires / audits.

6) Practical implementation: if we opt out of model improvement, what is the developer experience? e.g., API flag, tenant-level toggle, header, or contract-only? Any impact to caching, latency, or access to new feature improvements?

We appreciate concise answers and a short proposed DPA redline you can share.

Kevin — thanks for the clear list. High-level answers inline below; I'm attaching a proposed DPA with redlines and a SOC2 excerpt for your security team to review. I copied Monica (Customer Success) and Lauren (Legal) to help with any contract language.

1) Training opt-out (no-train): Short answer: yes — we offer a contractual commitment to exclude customer content from model improvement. Technically we support this two ways: a tenant-level account setting (for enterprise accounts) and an API-level request flag (DoNotTrain: true) that prevents content from being included in training pipelines. We will include the clause in the DPA.

2) Prompt/response ownership: We do not claim ownership of customer prompts or model outputs. Our standard DPA will state that customers retain rights to their content; Redwood receives a limited license to process the content for the purpose of providing the service only (and we will exclude it from improvement if the opt-out is set).

3) Subprocessors: See attached subprocessor list (and SOC2 excerpt). We provide 30 days' notice for new subprocessors and an opt-out path for material changes. For regulated customers we also offer Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) so data never leaves customer-controlled networks.

4) Cross-border transfers: For hosted customers we use SCCs for EU transfers and participate in the Data Privacy Framework where applicable. For US-only residency (PHI-adjacent) we recommend Redwood Private (or a Dedicated instance) to ensure all processing remains in US regions; we'll reflect transfer safeguards in the DPA.

5) Evidence: SOC 2 Type II excerpt attached. Security questionnaires can be routed to security@redwood.com; we can sign an NDA to share more detailed evidence if needed.

6) Developer experience: If you select opt-out the developer flow is one of these options: tenant-level toggle (console + API) or per-request header (DoNotTrain: true). The header is honored immediately; the tenant toggle applies account-wide. Opting out does not affect latency materially and we do not charge an extra fee for the opt-out on Hosted accounts. Note: some advanced features that rely on aggregated usage signals (e.g., adaptive quantization suggestions) may not be available if you opt out of telemetry required for those features.

Summary of commitments and mechanics (Orbital Health / OPP-4821):

- Contract: Redwood will include the following clause in the DPA: "Redwood shall not use Customer Content to train, improve, or adapt Redwood's models or model weights, nor include Customer Content in datasets used for model benchmarking, unless Customer provides explicit written opt-in."
- Technical enforcement: DoNotTrain is supported as a per-request header (DoNotTrain: true) and an account-level setting (console/API) that applies to all requests for the tenant.
- Auditability: Redwood will maintain an immutable audit log showing requests marked DoNotTrain and the exclusion actions for 12 months; excerpt samples are available on request.

2) Ownership and usage rights
- Customer retains ownership of prompts and generated outputs. Redwood's license is strictly to provide the service and is limited to processing and ephemeral caching necessary for serving responses. The DPA redlines clarify this language.

- Current subprocessors list is attached. Redwood provides 30 days' notice for new subprocessors. For material changes, we provide an opt-out pathway and will engage on alternatives (including Dedicated or Private deployments).

- For cross-border transfers we rely on SCCs for EU transfers and Data Privacy Framework where applicable. For US-only residency and PHI-adjacent workloads we recommend Redwood Private or a Dedicated US-only deployment; we'll reflect residency options in the DPA.

5) Evidence and audits
- Attached: SOC 2 Type II excerpt. Security questionnaires can be routed to security@redwood.com. We can provide further artifacts under an NDA and schedule a SOC walk-through if needed.

6) Developer experience and feature impact
- The opt-out will be honored in real-time with the DoNotTrain header or tenant toggle. There is no additional fee for the opt-out on hosted accounts. Note that certain aggregated, opt-in-only features (adaptive telemetry-driven suggestions) may not be available when telemetry is disabled at the tenant level.

Hi Jane —

Thanks, really helpful list. High-level answers here and I'm attaching a concise "evidence map" that maps each SLA/SLO line item to the telemetry we can provide. Quick summary: 

- Uptime definition: For hosted API we measure "service availability" based on the control-plane and dataplane success rate on the public REST endpoints used by customers (/v1/generate, /v1/chat, /v1/embed). We report a weighted availability metric per region based on successful 2xx responses over total production requests (excluding client-side 4xx). Health-checks are used for internal routing, but they are not the primary contractual signal.

- Latency measurement: We compute p50/p95/p99 on server-side response time from request-accept to final token emission (server processing + model time). Percentiles are computed on a rolling 24h window by default and on contract windows (monthly calendar) for SLA evaluation. We also provide a 1-minute and 5-minute rolling series for on-call debugging.

- Evidence set for crediting: For each incident we can provide: timeline (UTC), raw request ids (up to 1000 sample ids), per-request traces (latency buckets), backend kernel and model version, autoscale/queue metrics, and synthetic probe logs for the same time window. We will redact customer payloads unless a CDA is in place.

- Synthetic vs real traffic: Our standard approach is to correlate synthetic probe signals with sampled production traffic. For credit calculation we weight production traffic at 80% and synthetic probes at 20% by default; we can negotiate different weights or a rule that triggers 100% production-only evaluation if production sampling density crosses a threshold (e.g., >5 requests/sec aggregated over the region during the incident).

Attached: redwood_sla_evidence_map.pdf (mapping + example incident package) and a short SOC2 attestation summary. Turnaround for evidence: we commit to acknowledging requests within 1 business day and delivering a packaged evidence set within 5 business days for standard incidents. For complex multi-region incidents we propose a 10-business-day window (we'll flag those in our initial ack).

I'll loop in our internal SRE and legal reviewers to make sure we can provide the exact artifacts you need without exposing sensitive customer data. Do you have any preferred formats for the evidence bundle (e.g., CSV request list, zipped JSON traces, or a shared Drive folder)?

1) Evidence package format: CSV for request ids + metadata (timestamp, region, request_id, status_code, latency_ms), gzipped JSON traces for sampled requests, and an "Auditable Worksheet" (spreadsheet) that shows incident inputs and credit math. 2) Monotonic timestamps: request ids include server-assigned sequence numbers and RFC3339 timestamps (UTC) so timelines can be reconstructed. We will include mapping keys for frontend->backend hops where available.

Thanks Marcus — attaching the terms our procurement team pulled together (NeuroVista_Requested_Terms_v1.pdf). A few open items we need clarified before we can route redlines: 

1) How do you define a "capacity unit"? Our legal wants a single unambiguous conversion to hardware (e.g., "1 capacity unit = X GPU equivalent / Y vRAM-hours").
2) How do you measure throughput guarantees (is it vram-hours, GPU-hours, or tokens/sec)? We run a mix of short chat and long-batch inference so we care about both sustained throughput and burstability.
3) Service credit ladder — we prefer a cap on credits (insurance won't allow full refunds). Can you provide an explicit ladder with triggers, measurement windows, and cap?
4) Discount schedule — we'd like clarity on how line-item discounts map to committed SKUs vs. actual consumption (especially if we burst beyond reserved).

We're hoping to keep the commercials simple but need the contract language to be precise. Can you send your recommended definitions and an example calculation for our expected profile (roughly 4 A100-equivalent GPUs reserved, with 2x burst allowance)?

Attachments: NeuroVista_Requested_Terms_v1.pdf (requested terms)

Thanks,
Kyle Peters
Head of Platform Partnerships
NeuroVista Inc

High-level proposed definitions (working draft):
- Capacity Unit (CU): 1 CU = 1 vram-hour on an A100-80GB equivalent instance. For contract language we can also define as "1 CU = 1 GPU-PU (A100-80GB performance profile)" to avoid ambiguity across hardware families.
- Commitment accounting: Monthly commitment is expressed in CU-hours (e.g., 4 A100 equivalents reserved continuously for a 30-day month = 4 CUs * 24 * 30 = 2880 CU-hours/month).
- Throughput guarantee: Measured as two dimensions — (A) Sustained capacity: CU-hours available per monthly billing period; (B) Latency SLO: p50/p95 inference latency measured against a defined synthetic workload (seq len 256 chat mix) routed to the dedicated pool.
- Burst policy: Customers retain short-term burst allowance (up to 2x committed CU for up to 3 hours/day) as billable overage at the committed discount rate; we can offer an optional burst buffer (pre-purchased pool of CU-hours) to smooth billing.
- Service credits (draft ladder): See spreadsheet, summary below. Credits are applied prorata to monthly commit value and capped at a negotiated percentage.

I'll follow up with internal notes to align on credit ladders and discount table then send a redline-friendly clause set.

Internal notes / proposed redline items (please comment):

--- Forwarded message ---
From: Kyle Peters <kyle@neurovista.io>
Subject: Questions on Dedicated commit definitions and remedy ladder

1) Capacity Unit (CU): propose we define CU as "1 vram-hour of A100-80GB performance". This avoids vendor-specific model names but ties to perf profile. +1 to include exact micro-bench numbers in appendix.
2) Throughput: measure committed CU as capacity pool; SLA attaches to p50 latency on a defined synthetic profile. If p50 exceeds target for >X% of measured minutes, triggers credit.
3) Ladder: customer prefers a cap. Proposed ladder we should offer: 
   - Monthly uptime >= 99.9% --> 0% credit
   - 99.0% <= uptime < 99.9% --> 5% of monthly commit value
   - 95.0% <= uptime < 99.0% --> 15% credit
   - uptime < 95.0% --> 30% credit cap — propose we cap aggregate credits at 50% of monthly commit (internal concession to customer request).
4) Burst: allow 2x burst for up to 3 hours/day; bill as overage at committed unit price or allow pre-purchased burst pool at 60% of on-demand.

Open items for legal: explicit measurement window (we use rolling 5-minute measurement aggregated to daily), definition of "downtime" vs "degraded performance", and auditability (customers will ask for metric export and root cause write-ups).

Please weigh in on the following before I send to Kyle: 1) cap at 50% vs 100%; 2) 3-hour burst window vs 1-hour; 3) pre-purchase burst pool discounting (60% vs 75%).

--Marcus

Monica — recommend we push for 50% cap and 3-hour burst (improves our flexibility). Aditya — if pricing wants 60% for pre-purchase burst pool we might need to mark special pricing for >12mo commit. Lauren — confirm marketing/packaging language for "CU" and sample math is consistent with docs.

Subject: Proposed definitions and example math for NeuroVista commit

Kyle — thanks for the patience. Below is a concise, redline-friendly set of definitions and an example calculation based on your stated profile (4 A100-equivalent appliances reserved; 2x burst allowance). If this matches your intent we can turn it into contract clauses and circulate for signature.

Proposed definitions (final candidate wording):
- "Capacity Unit (CU)": a unit of reserved capacity equal to one vram-hour on a performance profile equivalent to NVIDIA A100-80GB. For clarity: one CU corresponds to the compute capacity required to serve the defined synthetic workload at p50 latency target on an A100-80GB equivalent device for one hour.
- "CU-hour": one Capacity Unit consumed for one hour. Monthly commitments are measured in CU-hours.
- "Committed CU-hours": the CU-hours the customer has prepaid/reserved for the monthly billing period.
- "Burst Allowance": a short duration allowance permitting the customer to exceed the Committed CU-hours rate by up to 2x for up to 3 hours per calendar day; overage beyond the Burst Allowance will be billed as described in the pricing schedule.
- "Throughput & Latency SLO": Redwood will measure p50 and p95 latency for a defined synthetic workload (seq len 256 chat mix). The p50 latency SLO applies to 95% of the measured samples in the monthly aggregation window.

Service credit ladder (measurement & remedy):
- Measurement window: rolling 5-minute intervals aggregated across the monthly period; incidents are reported with timestamped metrics and RCA within 5 business days.
- Ladder (applies to monthly invoice amount for the committed CU-hours portion):
   * Monthly availability >= 99.9%: 0% credit
   * 99.0% <= availability < 99.9%: 5% credit
   * 95.0% <= availability < 99.0%: 15% credit
   * availability < 95.0%: 30% credit
- Credit cap: aggregate credits for a single monthly billing period are capped at 50% of the monthly committed CU-hours value (negotiable).

Example commit math (worked example):
- Customer target: reserve 4 A100-equivalent devices continuously.
- Monthly CU-hour calculation: 4 CUs * 24 hours * 30 days = 2880 CU-hours/month.
- If NeuroVista uses additional burst beyond the Burst Allowance, overage billed at committed unit price (no surcharge) unless pre-purchased burst pool is used.
- If availability for the month measured at 98.4%: credit = 15% of monthly committed CU-hours value (per ladder). If the credit calculation would exceed 50% cap we apply the cap.

Attachments: redwood_capacity_mapping.xlsx contains mapping of common GPU classes to CU equivalents and sample pricing rows for 12/24/36 month commits.

Next steps: 1) confirm the 50% credit cap is acceptable; 2) confirm burst window (we suggested 3 hours/day); 3) we can produce contract-ready language for section: "Definitions — Capacity & Remedies" and attach as an amendment to your draft.

If convenient, I can book a 30m call today to walk through the example with procurement and contracts.

Regards,

- "CU-hour": one Capacity Unit consumed for one hour. Monthly commitments are measured in CU-hours.
- "Committed CU-hours": the CU-hours the customer has prepaid/reserved for the monthly billing period.
- "Burst Allowance": a short duration allowance permitting the customer to exceed the Committed CU-hours rate by up to 2x for up to 3 hours per calendar day; overage beyond the Burst Allowance will be billed as described in the pricing schedule.

- Measurement window: rolling 5-minute intervals aggregated across the monthly period; incidents are reported with timestamped metrics and RCA within 5 business days.
- Ladder (applies to monthly invoice amount for the committed CU-hours portion):
   * Monthly availability >= 99.9%: 0% credit
   * 99.0% <= availability < 99.9%: 5% credit
   * 95.0% <= availability < 99.0%: 15% credit
   * availability < 95.0%: 30% credit
- Credit cap: aggregate credits for a single monthly billing period are capped at 50% of the monthly committed CU-hours value (negotiable).

- Customer target: reserve 4 A100-equivalent devices continuously.

Alex — thanks for the flag and the docs. I reviewed their redlines. Summary of legal concerns:

- "Audit rights" as written are too broad: they request access to runtime internals, arbitrary personnel interviews, and unlimited third-party auditors.
- "No egress" language for backups & logs inside their account is acceptable technically but we need a clause that still allows Redwood to run monitoring agents for safety & support, and a carveout for incident response that can cross-account with explicit notice.
- Telemetry/PII: we should add explicit opt-in language and a technical appendix describing what telemetry is collected by default and how to disable it.

My recommended compromise (to present to Northridge):
1) Audit: one remote audit per 12 months + optional onsite once in the first contract year with 30 days' notice; audits are scope-limited to configuration, access controls, and archival procedures — no arbitrary runtime interrogation. Third-party auditors allowed only if pre-approved by Redwood and limited to approved scope.
2) Residency: accept VPC-only deployment with the caveat that Redwood will maintain limited support connectivity (mutual TLS) for incident response; any cross-account access requires a legal hold and 7-day notice.
3) Telemetry: include an appendix and opt-in for advanced telemetry; all telemetry pipelines must be scrubbed of PII by default.

Business ask: if we accept those concessions, recommend approving a one-time 12% commercial concession (discount) and require a minimum 12-month commitment + accelerated support add-on. If leadership won't permit 12%, we can cap at 10% and add a customer-funded SOC2 readiness assessment as a compromise.

I'm seeking leadership approval on the audit carveouts and the discount cap.

Hi team —

I reviewed the customer's tracked DPA and summarized follow-ups below. I also attached an internal redline (Redwood_DPA_v3_redline.pdf) that highlights where LumenCare's suggested carve would materially change our risk profile.

Summary of key points and proposed responses:
1) SCCs: Redwood will adopt the EU 2024 SCCs. We'll include an SCC Annex as an exhibit to the DPA. No change to commercial terms required.

2) Hosting carve (customer asks for EU-only residency):
   - Proposal A (preferred): For the pilot, Redwood will commit to EU-hosted primary and warm-standby nodes. Add an explicit Order Form clause: "Production workload and primary store shall be hosted in the EU region specified in the Order Form."
   - Limitation: We cannot guarantee failover will remain in-region in an operational emergency without a separate runbook and approval process. We'll offer a runbook commitment and a notification SLA.
   - If LumenCare insists on contractually binding full geofencing for all failover scenarios, we need an exception to be approved by Security + Infra and will likely require an additional fee.

3) Subprocessor list and notice: Monica will supply the current subprocessor inventory and our 30-day notice process. We'll provide a one-off review window for major subprocessor additions for a 12-month period post-execution.

4) Evidence requests (SOC2, KMS, export procedures):
   - SOC 2 Type II: available; we can provide a redacted report under NDA.
   - Encryption: KMS detail (we use cloud KMS with customer key support for Dedicated/Private; hosted customers use Redwood-managed keys) — Monica to provide tech note.
   - SFTP/export: ops runbook exists; will provide an abbreviated procedure and expected timelines.

Action items (owners + ETA):
- Laura: propose Order Form language for the hosting commitment + an exception clause (by 2027-05-16 EOD).
- Monica: subprocessor list, SOC2 NDA template pointer, KMS brief, and ops export runbook (by 2027-05-17).
- Ben: coordinate a Friday 5/14 30-min triage (confirm availability).

Attachment: Redwood_DPA_v3_redline.pdf (high-level legal comments).

If LumenCare wants to limit scope to pilot (EU production only) and revisit broader geofencing after go-live, we can accept that as a commercial solution without perpetual additional fee. If they want a hard-coded SLA and contractual geofencing for all scenarios, we will need procurement/ops escalation.

Thanks —
Laura Bennett
